raw_text:
Sacubitril/valsartan is the prototype angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), combining valsartan-mediated angiotensin II type 1 receptor blockade with sacubitril-mediated augmentation of endogenous natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, adrenomedullin and other vasoactive substrates. The concept followed disappointment with dual ACE–neprilysin inhibition: omapatrilat improved some haemodynamic outcomes but excess angioedema limited development, probably because both ACE and neprilysin metabolize bradykinin [1]. Pairing neprilysin inhibition with an angiotensin receptor blocker was therefore mechanistically attractive, and early hypertension studies showed greater blood-pressure and natriuretic-peptide effects than valsartan alone [2]. The pivotal heart-failure programme was designed to test whether this neurohormonal strategy could improve outcomes beyond ACE inhibition [3].

In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), PARADIGM-HF established sacubitril/valsartan as disease-modifying therapy. Among ambulatory symptomatic patients with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) ≤40% (later ≤35%) and elevated natriuretic peptides, sacubitril/valsartan reduced the primary composite of cardiovascular death or first heart-failure hospitalization versus enalapril, with parallel reductions in all-cause mortality and sudden death, despite more symptomatic hypotension and less cough or hyperkalaemia [4]. Subsequent analyses strengthened biological plausibility: fewer patients experienced clinical deterioration requiring intensification of therapy [5], and reductions in both sudden and pump-failure death were observed [6]. Patient-centred benefits were also evident, with slower worsening of health-related quality of life and fewer physical and social activity limitations [7,8].

Safety and comorbidity data have been central to implementation. In PARADIGM-HF, sacubitril/valsartan was associated with less severe hyperkalaemia among patients receiving mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists [9], and renal decline was generally slower than with enalapril, although symptomatic hypotension was more frequent [10]. In patients with diabetes, sacubitril/valsartan modestly improved glycaemic control and reduced initiation of insulin therapy, suggesting favourable metabolic effects beyond haemodynamics [11]. Biomarker studies showed early increases in BNP, as expected from neprilysin inhibition, but reductions in NT-proBNP, troponin and soluble ST2, consistent with lower wall stress and myocardial injury [12]. Open-label mechanistic studies linked NT-proBNP reductions with reverse cardiac remodelling [13], although EVALUATE-HF did not show significant improvement in central aortic stiffness versus enalapril over 12 weeks [14].

Practical initiation has been examined in multiple clinical contexts. TITRATION showed that both condensed and conservative uptitration strategies were feasible, with slower uptitration useful in patients previously receiving low-dose renin–angiotensin system inhibitors [15]. PIONEER-HF extended evidence to haemodynamically stabilized patients hospitalized for acute decompensated HFrEF, demonstrating larger NT-proBNP reductions than enalapril without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalaemia or angioedema [16]. TRANSITION further supported pre-discharge or early post-discharge initiation, although target-dose achievement remained limited by blood pressure, renal function and clinical frailty [17]. In contrast, the LIFE trial in advanced HFrEF did not show superiority over valsartan for NT-proBNP reduction and highlighted tolerability challenges in very sick patients [18]. Thus, ARNI therapy is best initiated when congestion is controlled and systolic blood pressure and renal function permit.

Evidence is more nuanced in heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction. PARAMOUNT showed greater NT-proBNP reduction and left atrial reverse remodelling than valsartan in HFpEF, generating enthusiasm for outcomes testing [19]. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary endpoint of total heart-failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death, but suggested heterogeneity, with greater apparent benefit in patients with LVEF below the normal range and in women [20,21]. Pooled analyses across PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF support a treatment gradient, with maximal benefit in HFrEF and diminishing benefit as LVEF rises, particularly above the mid-50% range [22]. Subgroup work in HFrEF also indicates broadly consistent efficacy across age groups, although hypotension, renal dysfunction and polypharmacy increasingly shape tolerability in older patients [23].

Sacubitril/valsartan may influence cardiac structure and functional mitral regurgitation. In the PRIME trial, it reduced effective regurgitant orifice area more than valsartan among patients with secondary mitral regurgitation and LV dysfunction, suggesting that reverse remodelling can translate into valvular improvement [24]. Outside classical heart-failure trials, UK HARP-III found no major renal advantage over irbesartan in chronic kidney disease [25], while PARAMETER showed greater central aortic pressure reduction than olmesartan in older patients with systolic hypertension [26]. Contemporary HFrEF management increasingly combines ARNI with beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors; DAPA-HF analyses suggest dapagliflozin benefit is preserved on background sacubitril/valsartan [27], and modelling indicates large lifetime gains from comprehensive quadruple therapy [28]. Current European and American guidelines therefore recommend sacubitril/valsartan as foundational therapy for symptomatic HFrEF, either replacing ACE inhibitor/ARB therapy or used de novo when appropriate, while giving weaker, phenotype-dependent recommendations in mildly reduced or preserved EF [29,30].
